_comments: MJ Academy module 7 -- Animal's two related-record collections.
This file is the module's payoff, and it is worth understanding what it replaces. In module 5
the Care & Health panel built its own RunView over Care Logs and folded every figure in
TypeScript. In module 6 the 'an animal cannot be listed Available without a completed
vaccination' rule built ANOTHER read of the same rows, with a hand-written filter string. Two
hand-rolled reads of one relationship, in two packages, neither aware of the other.
One JSON blob on the relationship row replaces both. CodeGen emits the declaration onto the
GENERATED entity class, so animal.CareLogs exists with no subclass and works in the browser as
well as on the server -- and one animal.Save() now writes the animal and its care logs in a
single transaction.
CareLogs -- Source 'database', because care logs are transactional records that no BaseEngine
caches; they must be read fresh. ReadOnly false and Load 'explicit' are the defaults for a
database collection, stated here rather than left implicit because this is a WRITABLE
collection and silence would read as an oversight.
OnRemove 'delete' is the ownership statement, and it is where 'owned by its parent' actually
lives -- a policy value on the relationship row, not an adjective in a lesson. A care log has no
meaning without the animal it describes, so removing one from the collection deletes the row,
and deleting the animal cascades to its logs first, inside the same transaction. Contrast the
Adoptions collections below.
No Sequence policy: care logs are events on a date, not positions in a list. CareDate DESC gives
the read order every screen wants (newest care first) without MJ renumbering anything.
WHY Load IS 'explicit' AND NOT 'lazy', WHICH IS THE THING PEOPLE GET WRONG. 'lazy' would let
animal.CareLogs.Items fill on first read with no await -- but it requires Source 'cache' AND
read-only, because a property getter cannot await, so only a synchronous read from an already
loaded BaseEngine cache can fill one. Care logs are database-backed and writable, so 'lazy' is
not available to them, and CodeGen rejects the combination rather than emitting a declaration
that compiles and silently never fills. That constraint is the reason module 6's vaccination
rule stays in ValidateAsync -- see the rule's own comment.

@lookup:MJ: Entity Relationships.EntityID=@lookup:MJ: Entities.Name=MJ: Animals&RelatedEntityID=@lookup:MJ: Entities.Name=MJ: Adoptions&RelatedEntityJoinField=AnimalID

_comments: Adopter -> Adoptions. The SAME entity, declared as a collection from the OTHER side.
This pair is the clearest demonstration in the module of what makes Adoption a different shape
from CareLog. Care Logs is a collection on Animal and nowhere else, because a care log belongs to
exactly one animal. Adoptions is a collection on BOTH Animal and Adopter, because an adoption is
meaningful from both directions -- and the two declarations are kept apart only by
RelatedEntityJoinField in the lookup below (AnimalID on the Animal side, AdopterID here).
OnRemove 'refuse' on BOTH sides, and this is the important contrast with CareLogs.
'refuse' makes Remove() throw. Detaching an adoption from its animal or its adopter is always a
bug: the row's entire meaning is the pair, so an adoption with one side removed is not a lighter
record, it is a corrupt one. 'delete' would be actively dangerous here -- pruning a family's
inquiry list would erase the adoption history of the animals involved, and a completed adoption
is permanent record that must survive an adopter moving away. 'orphan' cannot even be expressed:
both foreign keys are NOT NULL.
So the three OnRemove policies are not stylistic preferences. Each one is the honest answer to
one question -- does this record still mean anything once it is detached from this parent?
CareLog: no, delete it. Adoption: the question is malformed, refuse it.
